note: Curated from upstream documentation with explicit Hermes support. Eligibility requires more than 50,000 fetched public stars and a reviewed entry in assets/js/github-policy.js. Older ineligible write-ups remain stored but hidden. Examples and summaries are archive-authored; installation commands are documented upstream.

items.title: farion1231/cc-switch
items.summary: One desktop app to manage every harness you run — and it names Hermes Agent in its own headline.
items.detail:
WHY
Running more than one agent harness means more than one config, more than one set of provider keys, and no single place to see what is pointed where. cc-switch is a Tauri desktop app whose stated job is managing exactly that spread — its README headline lists Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, OpenCode, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent and MiniMax Code by name.

HOW
Install the desktop release for your platform, point it at the harnesses already on your machine, and switch the active provider or profile from one window instead of editing each harness's own config file.

USE CASE
You run Hermes for long-lived agent work and something else for quick edits. Instead of hand-editing two config files whenever you change provider, you flip it in one place and both follow.

Verified: Hermes Agent is named in the project's own README headline.

items.title: colbymchenry/codegraph
items.summary: A code index with an installer that configures the Hermes MCP connection.
items.detail:
WHAT IT DOES
CodeGraph maintains a code index that agents can query through MCP. Its installer explicitly detects Hermes and configures the connection.

HOW TO USE IT
Install the CLI, open a new terminal, and run codegraph install to connect Hermes. Run codegraph init inside each project to build its index. Restart Hermes to load the MCP server. Installing the CLI alone does not configure the agent or index a project.

USE CASE
Ask Hermes to investigate relationships in an unfamiliar repository using the project index. This is an archive-authored example; token and speed savings are not measured here.
items.snippet:
npm install -g @colbymchenry/codegraph
# In a new terminal:
codegraph install
# From the project you want to index:
codegraph init
cardPoints: Connect Hermes to CodeGraph through its MCP installer.
Index each project before asking codebase questions.

items.title: garrytan/gbrain
items.summary: Memory you own, shared across whichever agent you happen to be using.
items.detail:
WHY
Agent memory usually belongs to the harness, so switching tools loses it. GBrain's stated premise is the opposite: it stores explicit facts with their sources, supports corrections and withdrawal, and makes the same memory available across agents. Facts carry provenance, which means you can audit what it believes and why — rare in a memory layer.

HOW
Start with the keyless mode and keyword retrieval; add semantic search, synthesis and background enrichment when the corpus justifies it. Newer local brains ship a content root with memory skills that connected agents can join.

USE CASE
Facts about your own stack — deploy targets, naming rules, which service owns what — that you would otherwise re-explain to every agent, every session, forever.

Verified: the GitHub description names Hermes; the README describes cross-agent memory generally rather than a Hermes-specific integration.

items.title: thedotmack/claude-mem
items.summary: Compresses what happened into context that survives the next session.
items.detail:
WHY
Long agent sessions end and take their working knowledge with them. claude-mem is a persistent memory compression system: rather than replaying a transcript, it compresses sessions into retrievable context and injects the relevant part back when it matters.

HOW
Install it beside the harness and let it capture sessions; it exposes search tools over the compressed store. The repo documents a quick start, how it works, and its search tools.

USE CASE
Multi-day work on one feature, where the context that matters was established on day one and the agent no longer has it on day three.

Caveat, stated plainly: the README says "built for Claude Code". The GitHub description claims it works with Hermes among others, but the project's own documentation leads with a different harness — check it against your setup before relying on it.

items.title: ruvnet/ruflo
items.summary: A meta-harness: agent teams, memory, verification and cost control layered over a harness.
items.detail:
WHY
One agent doing everything hits a ceiling. Ruflo's framing is "Agent = Model + Harness" and it sells the layer above: planning, memory, agent teams, plugins, cost accounting and verification, with a fourteen-chapter guide explaining the progression from a first task to a working team.

HOW
Install from npm (ruflo). Start with a single task, then add memory and teams as the work justifies it — the documentation is explicitly staged that way.

USE CASE
Work that needs several roles — someone to plan, someone to implement, someone to check — and a record of what each cost.

Caveat, stated plainly: the README describes it as a meta-harness "for Claude Code and Codex" and does not name Hermes Agent. It is here for the pattern, not for a verified Hermes integration.

items.title: JuliusBrussee/caveman
items.summary: A documented Hermes launcher for more concise agent output.
cardPoints: Launch Hermes through the Caveman wrapper.
Use its concise-output workflow for routine agent tasks.
items.detail:
WHAT IT DOES
Caveman provides a CLI wrapper and concise-output workflow. The README explicitly documents Hermes integration through a custom provider and environment configuration.

HOW TO USE IT
Install the CLI, complete its setup, then launch Hermes using caveman hermes. Read the upstream setup notes for your provider.

USE CASE
Keep routine task responses short when verbose explanations make repeated runs harder to scan. This is an archive-authored example.

EVIDENCE
The archive verifies the documented integration, not the project’s claimed token savings. No savings figure is presented as a measured result here.
items.snippet:
npm install -g @caveman-ai/cli
caveman setup --install
caveman hermes

items.title: nexu-io/open-design
items.summary: Connect a local design engine to Hermes through MCP.
cardPoints: Connect OpenDesign to Hermes with its MCP installer.
Use the design engine for prototypes and visual artifacts.
items.detail:
WHAT IT DOES
OpenDesign exposes a design engine through its CLI and MCP integration. Its support table includes a dedicated Hermes configuration command.

HOW TO USE IT
Install OpenDesign and its od CLI using the upstream instructions for your platform. Then run the command below to configure the Hermes MCP connection. This command connects an existing installation; it does not install OpenDesign itself.

USE CASE
Ask Hermes to create a prototype or presentation artifact using the connected design tools. This is an archive-authored example.

SETUP NOTE
The README provides platform-specific installation instructions; follow those before configuring the connection.

items.title: unslothai/unsloth
items.summary: Launch Hermes with local models through Unsloth.
cardPoints: Use the documented Hermes launcher for local models.
Keep model setup and agent work in one local workflow.
items.detail:
WHAT IT DOES
Unsloth documents agent launchers and compatible model-serving APIs, including an explicit Hermes launcher. Its broader training and model tooling is not Hermes-specific.

HOW TO USE IT
Install Unsloth and configure a supported local model using its upstream instructions. Then use the Hermes launcher below. Model and hardware setup are prerequisites, not handled by this archive.

USE CASE
Try a local model with a Hermes workflow after setting up the model in Unsloth. This is an archive-authored example; performance depends on the selected model and machine.
